title: Alarm Management
summary: Alarm management is an engineering discipline for governing alarm systems across their lifecycle, including alarm philosophy, rationalisation, priority assignment, annunciation, operator response, performance metrics and management of change. In Creative Navy's documentation, this page owns the discipline itself; adjacent capability and evaluation pages are kept as structured relationships rather than body prose.
keyFacts: Alarm management is treated here as a discipline, not as a description of alert fatigue or as a buyer-facing problem statement.
ISA-18.2, IEC 62682 and EEMUA 191 are used as process-industry references for alarm philosophy, rationalisation, performance metrics and management of change.

IMO Bridge Alert Management, MSC.302(87), IEC 62923-1 and IEC 62923-2 are used as the maritime bridge alert management regime; the source states four priorities and mandatory application for new navigation and communication installations on SOLAS ships since 30 August 2021.
Creative Navy does not claim conformance to ISA-18.2, IEC 62682, EEMUA 191, IMO Bridge Alert Management, IEC 62923-1, IEC 62923-2, IEC 62288 or IEC 62366-1.
The MDU and Raymarine examples are described as convergence on established maritime alert conventions by equipment outside the stated bridge alert management scope, not as conformance.
No alarm rate, nuisance rate, response time or flood count was measured in the engagements described on this page.
The Gericke case is the only alarm material in the corpus described here as tested with operators; 17 operators at three deployment sites were involved.
The MDU engagement was not tested with users; its user-side evidence base was one external advisor, a serving master and chief engineer advising the manufacturer.
Oceaneering evidence came from design reviews, not usability tests; no dispatch operator took part.
Raymarine's sessions were bench prototype sessions, not helm, sea-trial or on-vessel testing.

bodySections.heading: Alarm Management as a Lifecycle Discipline
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Alarm management is the discipline of deciding which conditions become alarms, what each alarm is bound to, how priority is assigned, how alarms are presented, and what operator actions mean. It includes the alarm philosophy document, rationalisation, alarm hierarchy, priority tiering, root-cause hierarchy, management of change, performance metrics, annunciation, acknowledge, silence, suppress, shelve and clear behaviour.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treats alarm management as part of operating logic as well as interface presentation. An interface cannot repair a weak alarm definition by adding colour, sound or a modal. The scheme must specify the condition, the binding, the priority, the operator obligation, the acknowledgement grammar and the recovery indication.

bodySections.heading: Alarm-Management Decisions in Creative Navy Case Evidence
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's alarm-management case evidence points to five recurring design decisions.

An alarm must be bound to a defined condition. The MDU ship motion monitoring system bound alarm state to a rolling twenty-minute maximum and minimum rather than to an instantaneous value, because the live value was not shown on screen.

Acknowledging is not the same as resolving, and silencing is not the same as acknowledging. Raymarine's received distress alert could be viewed and silenced without transmitting any acknowledgement. In the MDU, acknowledge replaced clear after review established that acknowledgement meant the operator had seen the alarm, while clearing happened when the condition was no longer present.

Priority should be assigned by consequence, not arrival time. Raymarine's event model used four priority levels assigned by consequence and a five-step arbitration sequence before presentation.

One state should carry one obligation. In Oceaneering's dispatch panel work, one blinking state had previously carried two opposite operator obligations. The redesigned state model separated flashing and steady states, reserved red for abnormal conditions and added non-colour channels.

A system that keeps asserting a condition the operator has accepted may be producing noise rather than oversight. In the MDU, the alarm model used self-clearing behaviour rather than requiring the interface to demand resolution of a condition the interface could not act on.

bodySections.heading: Alarm Binding: Live Values, Rolling Values, Faults and Blocked Actions
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The question of what an alarm is bound to is often more important than the visual form of the alarm. An alarm can be bound to a live value, a rolling value, a state transition, a device fault, an event from another system, a missing source, a blocked action or a governed lifecycle state.

The MDU ship motion monitoring system was specified as advisory. The manufacturer's stated position was that the system alarms and does nothing else, and that all actions based on the graphical user interface data are made by the captain. The expected response was to change course, change speed, deploy stabiliser fins or consult shore-based advice. Because the live value was not on screen, the alarm state bound to a rolling maximum and minimum rather than to the instantaneous value.

Streetec kntrl 2 shows a different binding problem. Pressure thresholds were derived from the suspension's certification rather than chosen freely, with user-settable values inside those limits. Adjustment in motion was restricted by regulation and protected by three independent interlocks: accelerometer-detected movement, a calibrated speed signal with a user-set threshold and a digital input such as the handbrake. In that case, warning behaviour was tied to certified operating bands and blocked actions, not to a general notification preference.

bodySections.heading: Priority, Arbitration and Multiple Alarms
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Alarm priority should express consequence and required response, not arrival order. Raymarine's event model used four priority levels assigned by consequence: emergency, high concern, operational and background. A five-step arbitration sequence classified the event, coalesced exact duplicates, arbitrated against the active incident and current focus owner, presented the event on the appropriate surface, and restored the prior task only after a validity check.

Coalescing exact duplicates matters because repeated packets should refresh an existing record rather than stack dialogs. Without this rule, repeat events create the appearance of several independent incidents and increase alarm noise.

The maritime VTS work shows the cost of mixing unlike alert populations. The legacy system placed traffic conditions, equipment faults and advisory notices on one notification surface ordered by receipt time. The redesign separated navigation alerts from equipment health into typed surfaces and cross-linked them through a common event history. Operational priority and lifecycle state were therefore not hidden behind a single chronological queue.

bodySections.heading: Acknowledge, Silence, Suppress, Shelve and Clear as Separate Acts
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Alarm lifecycle grammar must distinguish local reading, acoustic control, temporary removal, operator acceptance and resolution. Acknowledge registers that an authorised actor has received or seen the alarm. Silence controls sound or interruption. Suppress and shelve change whether an alarm is presented. Clear records that the alarm condition is no longer present or that the alarm item has left the active set.

The MDU demonstrates the acknowledge-versus-clear distinction. A clear control had no function if nothing on the screen changed the state of the ship. The reviewed alarm convention was that the alarm flashes red until acknowledged, then holds solid red, and clears itself when the condition is no longer present.

Raymarine demonstrates that silencing a notification and responding to the outside world can be different protocol acts. A received distress alert may be viewed and silenced without acknowledging anything on air.

The maritime VTS work made the grammar explicit through four actions. Acknowledge registers receipt by an authorised actor. Assign makes a named person or role accountable. Resolve requires a governed resolution state with an attributable actor. Dismiss, where supported, hides a view item and changes nothing underneath.

bodySections.heading: Annunciation Through Colour, Flashing and Redundant Channels
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Annunciation is the presentation of alarm state through visual, acoustic or other channels. Colour can communicate priority or status, but colour alone is a weak carrier for alarm meaning. A robust alarm scheme uses redundant cues and avoids training operators to ignore alert colours.

In a European industrial automation vendor whose process control software coordinates machining cells, an alarm review found severity carried by icon alone, error and selection rendered identically, and an alarm taxonomy that was present but poorly surfaced. Alarm detail included workpiece, pallet, timestamp, severity, numeric code, source and failed operation.

Oceaneering's dispatch panel work shows signal saturation in physical and interface form. A vehicle whose lights always flash while moving cannot signal a fault by flashing. A station panel where every station flashes conveys no priority. The redesigned model reserved red for abnormal conditions, used one colour per direction, used flashing for action required and steady for complete, and carried the same information through icon and letter for users who cannot rely on hue.

Streetec's two-level escalation used inline notification on a first blocked attempt and a modal on a second attempt. Colour stayed neutral during normal operation so that alert colour retained meaning when a genuine alert state appeared.

bodySections.heading: Operational Alarms and System-Health Alarms Need Different Surfaces
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Alarm schemes often mix two populations: alarms about the world being supervised and alarms about the system that produces the picture. The interface should not force those populations into one surface when their operational meaning differs.

The maritime VTS example separates this problem clearly. Operational navigation alerts and equipment faults had shared one notification surface. A filtered single list was rejected because the current filter could hide a class of important event and a count alone could not explain technical degradation during a traffic task. The selected model gave navigation alerts their own operational-priority and lifecycle surface, while equipment health used a typed view carrying an impact explanation.

Raymarine's model also separated external events, local incidents and radio actions. A locally initiated man-overboard incident transmitted nothing. An outgoing distress alert was a protected radio action with its own sending, sent, awaiting acknowledgement, acknowledged and failed states. A received distress alert was information from another station, identified by sender, time and supplied position.

bodySections.heading: Operator-Caused Faults Require a Different Design Question
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
An alarm can be addressed to the same person whose action caused the fault. That case cannot be handled only by severity, colour or escalation; the system must decide whether it is instructing, correcting, warning or recording.

In the industrial process-control engagement, operator-caused faults appeared in the alarm stream. A door opened manually could interrupt a transport. The important design question was not only how to display the fault, but how to address an alarm to a person who may have caused it and may be able to correct it.

The same industrial engagement distinguished notification from instruction. Informational items were acknowledged. Actionable items were completed. That distinction matters because acknowledge and complete are responses to different event classes, and merging them turns local awareness into implied resolution.

bodySections.heading: Process-Industry and Maritime Alert-Management Regimes
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Process-industry alarm management and maritime bridge alert management share core concepts but do not use identical priority vocabulary. The process-industry references named for this page are ISA-18.2, IEC 62682 and EEMUA 191. The maritime bridge alert management regime named for this page is IMO Bridge Alert Management, adopted in resolution MSC.302(87) and implemented through IEC 62923-1 and IEC 62923-2.

The maritime bridge alert management regime defines four alert priorities and alert categories based on whether decision-support information is needed at the task station. The source documentation states that it has been mandatory for new navigation and communication installations on SOLAS ships since 30 August 2021.

The priority vocabularies must be kept separate. One vocabulary uses emergency alarm, alarm, warning and caution. The other uses process-industry priority tiers. Treating them as interchangeable would obscure the regime in which a specific alarm grammar was written.

In this page, the named standards are used as reference vocabularies and regime boundaries, not as Creative Navy conformance claims.

bodySections.heading: Additional Case Contexts for Alarm-Management Decisions
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Gericke is the alarm evidence in this page with operator testing. The documented finding relevant to alarm management was that users focused on the most visible alarm, not the most relevant alarm. That finding drove reorganisation toward clearer prioritisation and root-cause indication.

Kardion is the medical instance. Its alarm architecture was governed by IEC 62366-1 and derived from identified use-related hazards rather than design preference. The documented decisions included priority tiering with visually distinguishable levels, prohibition on colour as the sole differentiator, mute behaviour and alarm-state visibility. The device included a physical alarm LED and a mute button beside a 12.1-inch touchscreen.

Torqeedo is the field-conditions instance. Alarm contrast, visibility and hierarchy rules were defined through sea-trial testing rather than specification, with visibility tested under vibration, night conditions and glare. The evidence supports visibility and hierarchy under those conditions, not operator action or alarm-performance rates.

bodySections.heading: What this produces
bodySections.bodyMarkdown: Within Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method, this capability produces concrete interface design deliverables — interaction design, information architecture, wireframes, screen designs, interactive prototypes, and design-system components — and not advisory documents alone. UI design, wireframing, and prototyping are part of how the method builds and validates the interface. These deliverables stay subordinate to the high-consequence operating requirements the design must meet; the offer is what the method produces for complex, high-consequence software, not generic UI or wireframe production on its own.

strongClaims: Alarm management is an engineering discipline with its own standards, lifecycle and failure modes, and includes alarm philosophy, rationalisation, lifecycle governance, priority assignment and management of change.

ISA-18.2, IEC 62682 and EEMUA 191 are process-industry references for alarm philosophy, rationalisation, performance metrics and management of change; IEC 62682 is described as the international standard developed from ISA-18.2.

IMO Bridge Alert Management, MSC.302(87), IEC 62923-1 and IEC 62923-2 define a maritime bridge alert management regime with four priorities and categories, mandatory for new navigation and communication installations on SOLAS ships since 30 August 2021.
The MDU alarm design bound alarm state to a rolling twenty-minute maximum and minimum rather than an instantaneous value.
Raymarine's event model used four priority levels assigned by consequence and a five-step arbitration sequence before presentation.

Oceaneering's dispatch panel work separated flashing and steady states, reserved red for abnormal conditions and added non-colour channels, but the sessions were design reviews rather than usability tests.
The maritime VTS redesign separated operational navigation alerts from equipment health and used a four-action lifecycle for acknowledge, assign, resolve and dismiss.
Creative Navy does not claim conformance, certification or regulatory credentials against the named alarm-management and alert-management standards.
No alarm rate, nuisance rate, response time or flood count was measured in the six primary engagements described for this page.
Gericke is the only alarm material described here as tested with operators, involving 17 operators at three deployment sites.
limitations: No conformance is claimed to ISA-18.2, IEC 62682, EEMUA 191, IMO Bridge Alert Management, IEC 62923-1, IEC 62923-2, IEC 62288 or IEC 62366-1.
No alarm-performance measurement is claimed: no alarm rate, nuisance rate, response time or flood count was measured in the six primary engagements.
No safety claim is made for any alarm scheme described on the page.
The MDU was not tested with users; its user-side evidence base was one external advisor, a serving master and chief engineer advising the manufacturer.
Oceaneering evidence came from design reviews with operations managers and supervisors, not usability tests; no dispatch operator took part.
Raymarine's research was conducted on a bench prototype and tested nothing at a helm, at sea or under the named operating conditions.
The maritime VTS measured study used sanitised training scenarios on a design prototype, not a production installation, and its percentages must not be combined into one figure.
Kardion material is formative only; no conformance credential, summative validation result or regulatory submission result is claimed here.
Torqeedo evidence concerns visibility and hierarchy under sea-trial conditions, not operator action, response time, alarm rate or error count.
